1.pericope_label: A certain man planted a vineyard and let it out to husbandmen: the stone which the builders rejected

schools.summary: Lightfoot observes that the hearers knew the parable was against them, since the Jews boasted of being the Lord's vineyard, and supplies the marking of a fourth-year vineyard with coloured clods; Ellicott notes that this report sends the servants singly where the other groups them, seizing on the most vivid presentation; Robertson glosses the rare verb for wounding in the head.
Gill insists that no single person is meant by any of the servants but a set of men, the other report having the plural.
Henry keeps the parable at the level of tenancy, members of the church being God's tenants with a good landlord and a good bargain, and notes that the demand was neither hasty nor high.

Theophylact makes the hedge the law that forbade mingling with strangers, spaces the servants by period from Elias to Daniel, takes the casting out of the vineyard as the crucifixion outside the city, and reads the corner as joining Jews and Gentiles.

Pseudo-Jerome supplies the fullest key to the allegory, the vineyard Israel, the hedge the guardianship of angels, the winefat the law, the tower the temple, the husbandmen the priests, and reads the hope of reverence as irony; Bede offers rival identifications for hedge and winefat, reads the three servants as Moses, the Psalmists and the prophets, denies that the chiefs killed through ignorance rather than envy, and turns the whole into a moral about the vineyard each of the faithful receives on hire at baptism; Augustine reconciles the reports over who answered the closing question.

debates.question: What is the hedge about the vineyard?

positions.view: the law, which forbade mingling with strangers

outliers.claim: the going into a far country was no change of place: he seemed to go away so as to leave the husbandmen to their own free will, and God is said to doubt for the same reason

themes: And he began to speak unto them by parables. A certain man planted a vineyard, and set an hedge about it, and digged a place for the winefat, and built a tower, and let it out to husbandmen, and went into a far country.
And at the season he sent to the husbandmen a servant, that he might receive from the husbandmen of the fruit of the vineyard.
And they caught him, and beat him, and sent him away empty.
And again he sent unto them another servant; and at him they cast stones, and wounded him in the head, and sent him away shamefully handled.
And again he sent another; and him they killed, and many others; beating some, and killing some.
Having yet therefore one son, his wellbeloved, he sent him also last unto them, saying, They will reverence my son.
But those husbandmen said among themselves, This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance shall be ours.
And they took him, and killed him, and cast him out of the vineyard.
What shall therefore the lord of the vineyard do? he will come and destroy the husbandmen, and will give the vineyard unto others.
And have ye not read this scripture; The stone which the builders rejected is become the head of the corner:
This was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes?
And they sought to lay hold on him, but feared the people: for they knew that he had spoken the parable against them: and they left him, and went their way.

13.pericope_label: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s

schools.summary: Lightfoot makes three points about the coin, that it was Caesarean, silver rather than gold, and Roman rather than of Jerusalem, with a rabbinic story of a penny to be dropped down a well; Ellicott notes that this report uses the specific word for the questioners' sin but omits the name hypocrites; Robertson lays the three accounts of their fault side by side and observes that only here is the question doubled in the sharp form, shall we give or shall we not give.

Henry explains the pairing of the two parties by their opposite interests, so that either answer could be turned against him, and observes that it is no new thing for those at variance in everything else to join in a confederacy against Christ; he turns their compliment into evidence, since if they meant it their killing him was a sin against knowledge.

Theophylact reports two accounts of who the Herodians were, a sect holding Herod to be the Christ or else Herod's soldiers brought as witnesses; says the plot had a precipice on both sides and that the Fountain of wisdom escaped their snares; reduces the answer to the rule that what bears an image goes to him whose image it bears, and extends it so that the body's inevitable wants are as Caesar to each of us.

Bede thinks the question framed to draw the answer that tribute should not be paid, so the Herodians might hold him an author of sedition, describes the coin as worth ten smaller ones, and answers those who suppose the question about the image was asked from ignorance; he takes the things that are God's as tithes, first-fruits and oblations. Pseudo-Jerome compares the questioners to bees, honey in the mouth and a sting in the tail, and makes the second half the point, that we render ourselves to God since it is his countenance that is stamped on us.

positions.view: a sect who held Herod to be the Christ
a party that stickled for the Roman power, opposite to the Pharisees

outliers.claim: the inevitable wants of our bodies are as Caesar to each of us, so the body is to be given its own, food and raiment, and God the things that are God's

themes: And they send unto him certain of the Pharisees and of the Herodians, to catch him in his words.

And when they were come, they say unto him, Master, we know that thou art true, and carest for no man: for thou regardest not the person of men, but teachest the way of God in truth: Is it lawful to give tribute to Cesar, or not?
Shall we give, or shall we not give? But he, knowing their hypocrisy, said unto them, Why tempt ye me? bring me a penny, that I may see it.
And they brought it. And he saith unto them, Whose is this image and superscription? And they said unto him, Cesar’s.
And Jesus answering said unto them, Render to Cesar the things that are Cesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s. And they marvelled at him.

18.pericope_label: When they shall rise from the dead they neither marry: he is not the God of the dead, but of the living

schools.summary: Robertson notes the reproach is put here as a question expecting assent where the other report asserts it flatly, and remarks that the Sadducees posed as men of superior intelligence and were ignorant of the Scriptures on this very point, as much error still is among the educated; Barnes limits the conclusion, that the peculiar relation of marriage will not exist but that no recollection or recognition is thereby denied, and explains the citation by chapter subject; Ellicott adds that the reference to the bush names the section rather than the place.

Henry calls them the sceptics of that age rather than persecutors, whose design was on the doctrine, and thinks the case was meant to ridicule the law of the brother's widow, noting their subtlety in appearing to own the truth they meant to overthrow.

Theophylact names the two ignorances, that they supposed a restoration of bodies such as they are now and that they thought scattered limbs hard to rejoin; explains that marriage exists on account of our decay, for succession, and ceases where there is no decay; and rests the proof on the present tense, I am and not I have been.

The Gloss states the fault of the questioners, that they contradicted the Scriptures and derogated from the power of God; Bede grants the tale is fitly framed to prove the madness of those who assert the resurrection of the body, though such a thing might really have happened, and infers the rising of the body from the survival of the soul, since the body did good and evil along with it; Pseudo-Jerome reads the whole mystically, the woman as the synagogue deserted by the sevenfold Spirit, the bush as an image of hearers whose thorns the fire does not burn off, and finds the Trinity in the threefold naming of God.

debates.question: How does the argument from the bush prove the resurrection?

positions.view: from the present tense, I am, as though the patriarchs were present
by inference: the soul survives, and the body rose and fell with it

outliers.claim: the passage denies the relation of marriage in the resurrection but does not deny that there will be recollection of it, or recognition of each other as having stood in it

themes: Then come unto him the Sadducees, which say there is no resurrection; and they asked him, saying,
Master, Moses wrote unto us, If a man’s brother die, and leave his wife behind him, and leave no children, that his brother should take his wife, and raise up seed unto his brother.
Now there were seven brethren: and the first took a wife, and dying left no seed.
And the second took her, and died, neither left he any seed: and the third likewise.
And the seven had her, and left no seed: last of all the woman died also.
In the resurrection therefore, when they shall rise, whose wife shall she be of them? for the seven had her to wife.
And Jesus answering said unto them, Do ye not therefore err, because ye know not the scriptures, neither the power of God?
For when they shall rise from the dead, they neither marry, nor are given in marriage; but are as the angels which are in heaven.
And as touching the dead, that they rise: have ye not read in the book of Moses, how in the bush God spake unto him, saying, I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob?
He is not the God of the dead, but the God of the living: ye therefore do greatly err.

28.pericope_label: Which is the first commandment of all? Thou art not far from the kingdom of God

schools.summary: Lightfoot explains the rabbinic distinction between the law and the precept, so that the question is whether the ceremonial precepts stand first; Barnes calls this one of the very few candid inquiries made of him, and takes the verdict as evidence that the older law prepares the mind for the gospel; Ellicott hears in the scribe's reply the sincerity of admiration rather than the covert sneer, and calls the passage an addition of singular interest; Robertson notes that this report puts the man in a favourable light where the other says he was tempting.

Calvin allows the malice and still credits the change, since the man openly assents and so is not of the class whose obstinacy is incurable; and he answers the objection that sacrifices, belonging to the first table, should not rank below charity, by distinguishing naked and empty sacrifice from the thing itself.

Theophylact divides the commandment by the powers of the soul, the living, the natural and the rational, argues that the two commandments mutually contain each other, and insists the verdict shows the man was not yet perfect, since it is not said he is within the kingdom.

The Gloss refers the strength to the bodily powers; Pseudo-Jerome traces the question to the differing forms of the commandments in Exodus, Leviticus and Deuteronomy, and says two are brought forward as two paps on the breast of the bride, adding that he is not far who comes with knowledge, since ignorance is farther from the kingdom; Bede reports the standing debate between those who praised sacrifices and those who preferred faith working by love, and closes on the silence that follows, that the venom of envy may be overcome but can hardly lie quiet; Augustine reconciles the reports on whether the questioner tempted him.

debates.question: Did the scribe come sincerely or as a tempter?

positions.view: sincerely; one of the few candid inquiries made of him
as a tempter, but corrected by the answer he received
with malice, yet openly assenting afterwards

outliers.claim: being confuted in argument they ask no further questions but hand him to the Roman power: the venom of envy may be overcome, but can hardly lie quiet

themes: And one of the scribes came, and having heard them reasoning together, and perceiving that he had answered them well, asked him, Which is the first commandment of all?
And Jesus answered him, The first of all the commandments is, Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord:
And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength: this is the first commandment.
And the second is like, namely this, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. There is none other commandment greater than these.
And the scribe said unto him, Well, Master, thou hast said the truth: for there is one God; and there is none other but he:

And to love him with all the heart, and with all the understanding, and with all the soul, and with all the strength, and to love his neighbour as himself, is more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.
And when Jesus saw that he answered discreetly, he said unto him, Thou art not far from the kingdom of God. And no man after that durst ask him any question.

35.pericope_label: How say the scribes that Christ is the son of David? Beware of the scribes, which devour widows’ houses

schools.summary: Barnes takes the gladly hearing crowd as the poorer sort, the rich being too proud to listen, though the fault is not the gospel's; Ellicott corrects the rendering to the great body of the people and denies that social condition is in view; Robertson agrees it is the huge crowd and reads the moment strategically, the morning's attack having been a colossal failure.

Henry turns the passage into a charge against the teachers, who could say the Messiah was David's son but not explain how David called him Lord, and draws from it that truths should be quoted from our Bibles rather than our ministers, the waters being sweetest at the source; he is less confident of the crowd's gladness, since none is found wrought upon to follow, and guards long prayers from being discredited by those who abused them.
Theophylact says the false opinion is corrected because the Passion is near, and rests the correction on the source of the words, that David cannot have spoken without the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Pseudo-Jerome says he speaks openly of himself so that they may be inexcusable; the Gloss sets the two propositions side by side, David's Lord by the psalm and David's son by the scribes' teaching; Bede takes the subjection of the enemies as showing the unity of nature rather than the Son's weakness, keeps the argument in use against those who make the Christ a mere man of David's line, and bounds the warning about long clothing, since the intention and not the office is blamed, while describing men who take money from troubled consciences as though they would be advocates at the judgment.

debates.question: Who are the crowd that heard him gladly?

positions.view: the poorer sort, the rich being too proud to listen
the great body of the people; the stress is on number, not condition

outliers.claim: he was to them a lovely song of one who plays well on an instrument, and some of them may have cried crucify him afterwards, as Herod heard the Baptist gladly and yet cut off his head

themes: And Jesus answered and said, while he taught in the temple, How say the scribes that Christ is the Son of David?
For David himself said by the Holy Ghost, The Lord said to my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand, till I make thine enemies thy footstool.
David therefore himself calleth him Lord; and whence is he then his son? And the common people heard him gladly.
And he said unto them in his doctrine, Beware of the scribes, which love to go in long clothing, and love salutations in the marketplaces,
And the chief seats in the synagogues, and the uppermost rooms at feasts:
Which devour widows’ houses, and for a pretence make long prayers: these shall receive greater damnation.

41.pericope_label: This poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury

schools.summary: Barnes is careful that her gift is not called greater in value but greater in love and self-denial; Ellicott finds the point in the placing of the story, since a widow whose house had been devoured shows that she keeps the two commandments the scribes had just set above sacrifice; Robertson glosses the word for mite as peeled or thin and notes that what she gave was her livelihood, adding that it is a tragedy to see a stingy saint pose as giving the widow's mite.

Calvin estimates offerings by the feeling of the heart rather than the apparent value, encouraging the poor and rebuking the rich in the same breath, and refuses to let the probable misuse of the treasury spoil the act, since men's abuses cannot prevent sincere worshippers from doing what is holy.

Clarke observes that even the rich gave brass money, produces the rabbinic canon that none might put in less than two of these coins, so that the widow could not have given less and her poverty prevented more, and asks what we should think of a rich man throwing a handful of halfpence into a public collection.

Theophylact supplies the custom of giving for the priests, the poor and the widows, and reads the widow as the soul, which leaves the Satan it was joined to and casts in flesh and mind, the flesh by abstinence and the mind by humility.

Bede explains the word for treasury from its Greek and Persian parts and its double use for chest and porch, states the principle that God weighs the conscience and not the property, and allegorises the rich as Jews puffed up with the righteousness of the law and the widow as the simplicity of the Church, whose two mites are the love of God and of neighbour; Pseudo-Jerome puts himself in the parable, asking who the poor woman is if not himself and those like him, who cast in what they can and have the will to explain where they lack the power.

debates.question: In what sense did she cast in more than all?

positions.view: in proportion to means, and so in love and self-denial, not in value
because God weighs the conscience and the store it came from, not the property

outliers.claim: the rabbinic canon forbidding an offering of less than two of these coins means she gave the smallest sum the law allowed, and could give no less

themes: And Jesus sat over against the treasury, and beheld how the people cast money into the treasury: and many that were rich cast in much.
And there came a certain poor widow, and she threw in two mites, which make a farthing.
And he called unto him his disciples, and saith unto them, Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury:
For all they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living.
